Background Remote-sensing imagery is widely used for agricultural monitoring, disaster management, urban planning, forest monitoring, water-resource assessment, infrastructure mapping, and environmental analysis. However, most existing remote-sensing AI solutions are developed as isolated applications for a single predefined task, such as land-cover classification, object detection, visual question answering, or change detection. These systems often require users to understand satellite-data characteristics, GIS workflows, model selection, and task-specific parameters. Consequently, non-expert users may find it difficult to obtain meaningful information from satellite imagery through simple natural-language queries.

Many operational remote-sensing questions cannot always be answered reliably using a single optical image. Relevant information may be distributed across paired or multiple observations acquired at different times or by different sensors. Optical and multispectral imagery provides spectral and contextual information, whereas synthetic aperture radar (SAR) provides complementary structural information and supports day-and-night acquisition through cloud cover. Multitemporal image pairs are required to identify and interpret changes over time, while co-registered opticalâ€“SAR pairs can provide more complete and reliable information than either modality alone.

A general-purpose large language model (LLM) or vision-language model (VLM) cannot be expected to perform these specialised tasks reliably without adaptation to remote-sensing imagery, sensor characteristics, and domain-specific terminology. The proposed solution must therefore include remote-sensing fine-tuning or domain adaptation and may employ multiple specialised models for different tasks. BigEarthNet.txt will serve as the primary dataset for adapting imageâ€“text representations to multisensor remote-sensing data. VRSBench and RSVQA will be used to evaluate single-image captioning, grounding, and visual question answering, while CDVQA will be used to evaluate multitemporal change-based visual question answering.

The novelty of SatQuery AI lies in its agentic, query-driven framework. Instead of applying a single generic VLM, the system selects and executes suitable remote-sensing specialist models, validates inputs, combines their outputs, and returns an evidence-grounded response.

Description The objective is to develop SatQuery AI, a software-based agentic vision-language assistant for analysing single and paired remote-sensing images through natural-language queries. Single-image understanding is a mandatory baseline, while the principal focus is joint reasoning over paired cross-modal and multitemporal imagery.

Defined Input Scope

• Single image: One optical/multispectral or SAR image for captioning, visual question answering, and text-guided region grounding.
• Cross-modal pair: Co-registered optical/multispectral and SAR images of the same geographic area for joint information extraction and cross-modal analysis.
• Bi-temporal pair: Two spatially corresponding images of the same geographic area acquired at different times for change detection, change description, and change-based visual question answering.
• Supported formats: GeoTIFF or TIFF for geospatial imagery. PNG and JPEG inputs may be accepted only for the prescribed public benchmark datasets.

Mandatory Functional Scope

• Remote-sensing adaptation: At least one visual or vision-language component must be fine-tuned or otherwise adapted using BigEarthNet.txt or the any open source training data.
• Single-image baseline: Visual question answering shall be mandatory. Each solution must additionally implement either captioning/scene description or text-guided region grounding.
• Multi-image change analysis: Change description or change-based visual question answering from a bi-temporal image pair shall be mandatory. A spatial change map may also be generated where reference masks are available.
• Cross-modal pair analysis: The system must extract complementary information from a co-registered optical/multispectral and SAR image pair.
• Agentic orchestration: The system must automatically select, sequence, and execute the appropriate specialist models or tools according to the query and input configuration.

Representative Queries

• 'Describe the land-cover and major objects visible in this image.'
• 'Highlight the water body referred to in the query.'
• 'What changed between these two dates, and where did the change occur?'
• 'Use the optical and SAR images together to identify built-up and water-covered regions.'
• 'Has the built-up area increased, decreased, or remained unchanged?'

Agentic Model and Tool Orchestration The system may use multiple specialised components, such as a remote-sensing VQA or captioning model, a grounding model, a change-understanding or change-VQA model, and an opticalâ€“SAR fusion or information-extraction model.

• interpret the query and classify the requested task;
• check the number, modality, format, metadata, and compatibility of the input images;
• select one or more models or tools from a predefined registry;
• configure only permitted task parameters and execute the selected workflow;
• combine textual and spatial outputs, estimate confidence, and return visual evidence; and
• provide an auditable execution summary containing the selected task, model/tool names, and key parameters.

The controller may perform internal task planning; however, only the observable execution trace, including the selected task, models or tools, permitted parameters, and outputs will be evaluated. Internal reasoning text is neither required nor evaluated.

Expected Solution The expected solution is an interactive GUI or web application with an agentic remote-sensing AI backend. It should accept supported image inputs and natural-language queries, select the appropriate specialist workflow, and return evidence-grounded textual and visual results.

The solution should include:

• Input upload and compatibility checking.
• A remote-sensing-adapted vision-language component.
• Specialist tools for VQA, captioning or grounding, change understanding, and opticalâ€“SAR analysis.
• An agentic controller for task routing, tool execution, and output integration.
• Visual evidence, confidence information, execution summaries, and downloadable reports.

Each solution must demonstrate single-image VQA, one additional single-image task, multitemporal change understanding, opticalâ€“SAR paired-image analysis, and agentic model/tool orchestration. A generic LLM or VLM without remote-sensing adaptation will not satisfy the requirements.

Deliverables An interactive GUI or web application with an agentic remote-sensing AI backend, Codes and models including test and demonstration.

Implementation Scope The system shall support single optical/multispectral or SAR images, co-registered opticalâ€“SAR pairs, and bi-temporal pairs in GeoTIFF/TIFF or approved benchmark formats. It must perform single-image VQA, one additional single-image task, change analysis, opticalâ€“SAR joint analysis, and agentic model/tool selection through an interactive GUI or web application.

Evaluation/Judging Criteria Final evaluation will use prescribed public benchmark test subsets and an ISRO/SAC evaluation dataset. Scores will be normalised before combining different metrics.

Add 'Evaluation/Judging Criteria' table here Public benchmarks will be evaluated using the prescribed test splits. The ISRO/SAC evaluation set will contain pre-georeferenced and co-registered Cartosat-2S optical and RISAT SAR image pairs, with task-specific reference answers, labels, bounding boxes, or masks, as applicable. Evaluation annotations will not be disclosed to participating teams.

Here is the structured breakdown of how every requirement, constraint, and evaluation metric in this statement maps directly to the architecture and implementation of **SatQuery AI**:

---

### 1. Architectural Alignment Matrix

| PS Mandate Component | Official ISRO/SAC Requirement | SatQuery AI Architectural Realization |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Agentic Paradigm** | Query-driven agentic framework selecting & executing specialist models rather than a monolithic black-box VLM. | **Careful Coordinator Pattern:** Dynamic task router classifies intent, validates metadata gates, sequences specialist tools, and returns evidence-grounded outputs. |
| **Observable Trace** | Auditable execution summary (selected task, models/tools, parameters, outputs). Internal thought text not evaluated. | **Observable System Provenance (`provenance.json`):** Strict JSON audit trail recording tool IDs, hardware profile, parameters, bounding boxes, IoU, and wall-clock latencies. |
| **Primary Datasets** | Adaptation on **BigEarthNet**; evaluation on **VRSBench**, **RSVQA**, and **CDVQA**. | Pre-configured data loaders & evaluation harnesses mapped to BigEarthNet-S2/S1, VRSBench (grounding/VQA), and CDVQA benchmarks. |
| **Spaceborne Imagery** | Pre-georeferenced & co-registered **Cartosat-2S** (optical) and **RISAT / EOS-04** (SAR) pairs. | Dual-stream engine handling optical reflectance (VNIR) alongside C-band SAR backscatter ($\sigma^0$ in VV/VH). |
| **Geospatial Formats** | **GeoTIFF / TIFF** for geospatial workflows; PNG/JPEG allowed for public benchmarks. | Full GDAL/Rasterio geospatial pipeline preserving Affine transform matrices, EPSG CRS projections, and radiometric depth (16-bit to float). |

---

### 2. Mandatory Functional Scope Checklist

```
[✔] 1. Remote-Sensing Adaptation
    └── Domain-adapted vision-language backbone trained on multisensor RS data (BigEarthNet).

[✔] 2. Single-Image Baseline (Mandatory VQA + Grounding / Captioning)
    ├── Task 1: Remote Sensing Visual Question Answering (RSVQA / VRSBench)
    ├── Task 2: Multi-scale Scene Captioning
    └── Task 3: Text-guided Visual Grounding ([xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax] + polygon contours)

[✔] 3. Bi-Temporal Multi-Image Change Analysis ($T_1 \to T_2$)
    ├── Change Detection & Spatial Difference Masks (Pixel/segment level)
    ├── Change Captioning (Natural language description of what changed)
    └── CDVQA (Change-based Visual Question Answering)

[✔] 4. Cross-Modal Pair Analysis (Optical + SAR Synergy)
    ├── Optical stream: Spectral and context information (land cover, vegetation, water albedo)
    ├── SAR stream: Structural roughness, moisture, dielectric contrast, cloud-penetration
    └── Joint extraction: Resolves ambiguity under cloud cover, shadows, or flood conditions

[✔] 5. Agentic Orchestrator & Execution Engine
    ├── Query Interpreter & Task Classifier
    ├── Data Readiness & Metadata Compatibility Gate (CRS, spatial overlap, resolution)
    ├── Tool Registry Execution
    ├── Output Integration & Confidence Estimation
    └── Interactive Web/GUI with Split-Screen & Downloadable PDF/JSON Reports
```

---

### 3. Key Operational Rules Emphasized by the Mandate

1. **No Monolithic Hallucinations:** Unconstrained general-purpose VLMs will fail the evaluation. Specialization, fine-tuning, and deterministic metric calculation (e.g., area in $\text{km}^2$ computed via geospatial affine resolution rather than token prediction) are essential.
2. **Evaluated on Observable Provenance:** The judges grade the **execution trace** and results, not internal reasoning strings. The system must output clean, structured, auditable metadata.
3. **Readiness & Compatibility Checks:** The pipeline must verify image compatibility (coverage overlap, matching or reprojectable CRS, temporal order) before triggering inference.

---

### What would you like to focus on next?
1. **Model Adaptation & Benchmark Pipeline:** Set up fine-tuning/inference scripts for BigEarthNet, VRSBench, RSVQA, and CDVQA.
2. **Interactive UI & Split-Screen Viewer:** Build or refine the web application for single, bi-temporal, and optical–SAR inspection.
3. **Agentic Orchestrator & Tool Registry:** Solidify the router, validation gates, and observable provenance logging.

SATQUERY AI — FINAL AUTHORITATIVE BUILD SPECIFICATION (v3)
============================================================

You are the senior AI/ML + geospatial + full-stack engineer
responsible for implementing:

SATQUERY AI
"An Interactive Vision-Language Assistant for Multimodal Remote

This is the final, locked specification. It supersedes all earlier
drafts. Read Section 0 and Section 42 (Antigravity Execution
Protocol) before doing anything else.

============================================================
0. NON-NEGOTIABLE ENGINEERING PRINCIPLES
============================================================

Build SatQuery AI as an evidence-driven, agentic remote-sensing
analysis system.

It must NOT be implemented as:

    User → generic LLM → answer

It must instead operate as:

    UNDERSTAND → CHECK → CHOOSE → ANALYZE → VERIFY → EXPLAIN

The system must understand the user's query, inspect the supplied
remote-sensing data, determine which specialist capability is
required, execute the appropriate tools/models, verify the result
against computational evidence, and present the answer with visual
evidence, confidence, and execution provenance.

No specialist model is allowed to become a single point of failure.

Every mandatory PS capability must have an executable baseline
implementation independent of optional large-model inference. Large
RS-VLMs improve the system when available. They must NEVER determine
whether the core SatQuery application can start, accept data,
validate data, route tasks, perform deterministic analysis, produce
evidence, show execution traces, or generate reports.

THE GOLDEN RULE:

    The planned architecture is not evidence that a capability
    exists. A capability becomes "implemented" only after its code

Never report a feature as complete merely because its code exists.

19. Clean separation of training/validation/public test/hidden test.

      └── demo_fallback

    single_image_grounding
      ├── geochat
      └── demo_fallback

    temporal_change
      ├── deterministic_change_engine      (always required — Section 16)
      ├── changechat                       (optional explanation layer)
      └── demo_fallback

    optical_sar_analysis
      ├── optical_sar_fusion_engine        (always required)
      └── croma_enhanced_analyzer          (optional)

Every capability entry must declare: name, task, supported

============================================================
8. FINAL MODEL REGISTRY
============================================================

------------------------------------------------------------
8.1 GeoChat
------------------------------------------------------------

Primary specialist for single-image VQA, RS image understanding,
grounding, region-level understanding, captioning where supported.

Do not replace it with a generic LLaVA/CLIP/chat model merely
because integration is easier. If unavailable, activate the
registered fallback — never claim the fallback is equivalent.

------------------------------------------------------------
8.2 ChangeChat — OPTIONAL, HYBRID mode is the EXPECTED default
------------------------------------------------------------

ChangeChat requires approximately 48GB-class NVIDIA GPU memory per
its own published hardware requirements. This rules out essentially
all single consumer GPUs (3090, 4090, most laptop GPUs — 24GB or
below). Treat it as the exception, not the norm.

ChangeChat integration should only proceed if, in this exact order:

    1. the License Gate (Section 4.1) passes;
    2. the checkpoint can legally be used;
    3. the team has access to suitable GPU compute (Profile A);
    4. the model passes the actual preflight inference test.

If any step fails: mark ChangeChat unavailable and continue.
Deterministic Change Engine = the production temporal engine, full
stop. ChangeChat, when available, is only an optional
language/explanation enhancement layered on top of it.

**The SIH demo must be fully convincing without ChangeChat.** Do not
design the presentation or the team's expectations around it being
available.

Give ChangeChat a hard integration/debugging budget of 3 hours,
starting only after the License Gate passes. If unsuccessful after
that budget, mark unavailable and move on — do not sacrifice the
project for one model.

------------------------------------------------------------
8.3 Deterministic Change Engine — MANDATORY, ALWAYS REQUIRED
------------------------------------------------------------

Must work completely independently of ChangeChat.

    T1 + T2 → metadata validation → spatial registration →
    common grid → change computation → thresholding →
    mask cleanup → connected components → geometry → measurement

Output structured evidence, e.g.:

    {
      "change_detected": true,
      "regions": [...],
      "changed_area": ...,
      "unit": "...",
      "mask_path": "...",
      "bbox": [...]
    }

No LLM-generated numerical value may override this result.

------------------------------------------------------------
8.4 Optical-SAR Fusion Engine — MANDATORY
------------------------------------------------------------

Do NOT make CROMA a requirement for this capability.

    Optical → optical feature extraction → optical evidence
    SAR     → SAR feature extraction     → SAR evidence
    optical evidence + SAR evidence → spatial fusion →
    fused result → confidence

Optical evidence candidates: RGB/false color, NDVI, NDWI, NDBI,
spectral ratios — only use an index if the necessary bands exist;
never assume all optical imagery has the same bands.

SAR evidence candidates: backscatter, polarization, texture,
relative intensity, spatial patterns. Do NOT use universal
hard-coded SAR thresholds — thresholds must be configurable,
documented, and validated on development data, never claimed to be
physically universal.

------------------------------------------------------------
8.5 CROMA — OPTIONAL, stretch only
------------------------------------------------------------

CROMA produces multimodal representations. It does NOT automatically
constitute a water/built-up/change detector. If used for a
downstream task, implement and document the actual task-specific
head. Never write "CROMA detected water" unless an implemented task
head actually produced that result. If CROMA integration causes
dependency or compute problems, disable it without affecting
mandatory functionality.

============================================================
9. INPUT GATEWAY
============================================================

Support: GeoTIFF, TIFF, PNG/JPEG only where permitted by the
relevant benchmark/demo.

For each raster extract: dimensions, CRS, transform, bounds,
resolution, band count, band metadata, nodata, acquisition time if
available, modality, sensor metadata where available.

Reject: corrupted files, unsupported formats, missing required
inputs, incompatible pairs, insufficient bands for the requested
operation, missing timestamps for temporal analysis.

============================================================
10. DATA READINESS GATE
============================================================

Build: RasterInspector, CompatibilityChecker, TemporalChecker,
CoRegistrationChecker.

For pairs check: CRS, bounds, spatial overlap, dimensions,
resolution, affine transform, acquisition timestamp, nodata,
modality, band availability.

If reprojection/resampling is required, perform it explicitly and
record source CRS, target CRS, resampling method, output resolution.
Never silently modify input data.

============================================================
11. QUERY CONTRACT
============================================================

Convert natural language into structured intent, e.g.:

    {
      "intent": "temporal_change",
      "requires_temporal_pair": true,
      "requires_spatial_evidence": true,
      "requested_outputs": ["description", "change_region"],
      "measurement_required": false
    }

Supported task types: single_image_vqa, single_image_grounding,
single_image_caption, temporal_change, optical_sar_analysis,
unsupported.

============================================================
12. AGENTIC ROUTER
============================================================

The controller must automatically determine: what task is being
requested, what inputs are available, what capability satisfies the
task, whether that capability is available on this machine, what
fallback exists, and what tool sequence is required.

If a required input is missing, refuse the task with a technical
explanation:

    Cannot perform temporal change analysis.
    Reason: Only one acquisition was supplied.
    Required: Two temporally distinct observations.

Do not hallucinate missing observations.

============================================================
13. GEOCHAT IMPLEMENTATION
============================================================

Implement single-image RS VQA first (image + question → answer,
confidence where available, model name, evidence, provenance), then
grounding (bbox/region + overlay + confidence + textual
description). Captioning can be added when supported.

============================================================
14. BIGEARTHNET.TXT ADAPTATION — THREE-TIER STRATEGY
============================================================

Do NOT download the entire corpus during the hackathon.

Tier 1 — Metadata: annotations, IDs, splits, task labels,
references. Goal: construct a reproducible manifest.

Tier 2 — Development subset: ~1,000–5,000 image pairs, sized to
disk/bandwidth/GPU/training time actually available. This is an
engineering development subset, not a claim of scientific
sufficiency.

Tier 3 — Task-filtered subset: filter for the actual adaptation
task. Recommended first task: image + question → answer. Example
split: 1,000–3,000 training, 200–500 validation, adjusted to actual
resources. Never fabricate dataset counts — record the actual
counts used.

============================================================
15. LoRA / PEFT
============================================================

Adapt the selected RS-VLM using PEFT/LoRA where technically
compatible. Record: base model, adapter configuration, dataset
version, exact train/validation counts, epochs/steps, learning rate,
batch size, gradient accumulation, hardware, checkpoint, evaluation
results. Report BASELINE and ADAPTED separately. Do not claim
improvement unless measured. If training cannot complete due to
compute, report that honestly and continue using the available
RS-adapted model as-is. Never fabricate a fine-tuning result.

============================================================
16. TEMPORAL CHANGE PIPELINE — DETERMINISTIC-FIRST ARCHITECTURE
============================================================

This is the corrected, final flow. The deterministic engine is not a
fallback bolted onto ChangeChat — it is the primary path, with
ChangeChat as an optional branch:

                 BI-TEMPORAL QUERY
                        │
                        ▼
              Compatibility / Registration
                        │
                        ▼
               Deterministic Change Engine
                        │
              ┌─────────┴─────────┐
              ▼                   ▼
        Change Mask          Geometry / Area
              │                   │
              └─────────┬─────────┘
                         ▼
                  Evidence Store
                         │
              ┌──────────┴──────────┐
              │                     │
        ChangeChat available   ChangeChat NOT
        (License Gate passed,   available
         Profile A GPU,              │
         preflight PASS)             │
              │                      │
              ▼                      ▼
      ChangeChat explanation   Template/rule-based
      layered on top of the    explanation generated
      verified mask/measurement   from the verified
                                    mask/measurement
              │                      │
              └──────────┬───────────┘
                          ▼
                   Verified Answer

ChangeChat explains evidence; it must never invent it. Example
structured result consumed by the explanation layer:

    {
      "change_detected": true,
      "changed_area": 2.81,
      "unit": "hectares",
      "regions": [{"id": "change_001", "bbox": [...], "area": 1.74}]
    }

============================================================
17. OPTICAL-SAR ANALYSIS
============================================================

Build OpticalSARAnalyzer: validate metadata → validate spatial
compatibility → co-register → create common grid → extract optical
evidence → extract SAR evidence → perform spatial fusion →
calculate evidence-level confidence → produce structured result →
generate explanation. Confidence must not be presented as a
calibrated probability unless calibration has actually been
performed.

============================================================
18. EVIDENCE STORE
============================================================

Every important claim must have evidence, e.g.:

    {
      "claim": "A water body is present",
      "source": "optical_sar_fusion",
      "evidence_type": "region",
      "bbox": [...],
      "confidence": 0.84,
      "model": "optical_sar_fusion_engine",
      "inputs": ["optical_01", "sar_01"]
    }

Evidence types: region, bbox, mask, measurement, metadata,
model_output, temporal_difference.

============================================================
19. NUMERICAL GUARD
============================================================

The language model must NEVER invent measurements. The measurement
engine computes the number; the response generator receives it; the
LLM may only verbalize a value it was given. Same rule for area,
pixel count, coordinates, distances, dates, resolutions, confidence
values, counts.

============================================================
20. VERIFICATION ENGINE
============================================================

Implement EvidenceVerifier, checking numerical consistency, region
consistency, mask existence, bbox validity, input provenance,
temporal consistency, output provenance, model/tool availability. If
verification fails, mark the result as uncertain rather than
silently producing a confident answer.

============================================================
21. EXECUTION TRACE
============================================================

The system must expose an observable execution trace (facts, never
hidden chain-of-thought):

    EXECUTION TRACE
    ✓ Input validation
    ✓ GeoTIFF metadata extracted
    ✓ Query classified: TEMPORAL_CHANGE
    ✓ Temporal pair validated
    ✓ Images aligned
    ✓ Change detector executed
    ✓ ChangeChat executed (or: fallback explanation used)
    ✓ Measurements verified
    ✓ Evidence overlay generated
    ✓ Final response generated

Also show the selected tools list.

============================================================
22. GUI
============================================================

Frontend: React/Next.js. Backend: FastAPI. ML: PyTorch, Transformers,
PEFT. GIS: Rasterio, GDAL, GeoPandas, Shapely, pyproj. Visualization:
Leaflet/OpenLayers/MapLibre or a practical equivalent.

Screen 1 — Upload: file upload, detected modality, CRS, dimensions,
resolution, bands, timestamp, compatibility status.
Screen 2 — Query: natural-language query box.
Screen 3 — Analysis: answer, confidence, image, evidence overlay,
before/after, masks/bboxes, execution trace, **runtime mode
indicator**.
Screen 4 — Report: download PDF, JSON, GeoJSON, masks.

============================================================
23. REPORT FORMAT
============================================================

Generate report.pdf, result.json, execution_trace.json,
evidence.geojson, change_mask.tif. PDF sections: query, input data,
sensor/modality info, task selected, models/tools executed, result,
visual evidence, measurements, confidence, limitations, execution
trace.

============================================================
24. PUBLIC DATA / EVALUATION
============================================================

Maintain strictly separate TRAIN / VALIDATION / PUBLIC TEST / HIDDEN
TEST. Never use hidden ISRO/SAC evaluation data for training,
fine-tuning, threshold tuning, model selection, prompt optimization,
or manual parameter tuning. Public evaluation sources: RSVQA,
VRSBench, CDVQA, BigEarthNet.txt — use each benchmark's own
prescribed splits. Do not invent benchmark numbers.

============================================================
25. METRICS
============================================================

Report task-specific metrics only: VQA (accuracy/exact-match),
captioning (benchmark-appropriate metric), grounding (IoU/mAP),
change (IoU/F1/precision/recall/change-QA metrics), segmentation
(IoU/Dice), optical-SAR (task-specific), agent (routing accuracy,
task completion rate, invalid-input handling rate), system (latency,
memory, model availability). Do not combine unrelated metrics into a
homemade score unless the official evaluation requires it.

============================================================
26. LEAKAGE CONTROL
============================================================

Prevent source/variant leakage — do not allow visually related
variants from the same source to cross train/test splits. Keep
training/validation/public test/hidden test strictly separated and
document the split logic.

============================================================

DEMO 1 — Single-image VQA: upload optical image, ask a land-cover
question → RS-VLM answer + evidence + confidence + trace.

+ overlay + answer + confidence.

DEMO 6 — Failure handling: one image only, "What changed?" → precise
refusal, no hallucinated second observation.

============================================================

============================================================

polarization, a universal spatial resolution, universal SAR
backscatter thresholds, universal cloud behavior, or universal

limitation if a required property is missing. SAR calibration must
be metadata/product-aware — never a universal DN → sigma0 formula.

============================================================

configuration files, environment variables, unit tests, integration

frontend.

============================================================

GeoChat is a grounded Large Vision-Language Model (VLM) tailored for remote sensing, built upon the **LLaVA-1.5** architecture[1][2][3]. 

### Hardware Requirements
Because GeoChat is based on the LLaVA-1.5 framework, its resource requirements generally align with those of similar 7B-parameter vision-language models[1][2].

*   **Training Requirements:** The official repository notes that the original model was trained on **3 x A100 GPUs (40GB memory each)**[1][4]. The documentation suggests that if you have fewer or less powerful GPUs, you can adjust the `per_device_train_batch_size` downward and increase the `gradient_accumulation_steps` to compensate, provided the global batch size remains constant[1][4].
*   **Inference (Running the Model):** While official VRAM minimums for inference are not explicitly listed in the repo, LLaVA-1.5 7B models typically require:
    *   **~14–16 GB VRAM** for running at full 16-bit precision[5].
    *   **~6–8 GB VRAM** if using 4-bit quantization (a common practice to run such models on consumer-grade hardware)[5].
    *   **Frameworks:** To optimize performance, the repository recommends using **Flash Attention** (`flash-attn`), which significantly reduces memory overhead during both training and inference[1][4].

### Getting Started
*   **GitHub Repository:** [mbzuai-oryx/GeoChat](https://github.com/mbzuai-oryx/GeoChat)[1][2]
*   **Environment:** The project typically requires a Linux-based environment with Python 3.10 and CUDA support[1]. It is recommended to use `conda` to manage the environment and install dependencies as outlined in their `README.md`[1][4].
*   **Key Dependencies:**
    *   `transformers`
    *   `flash-attn` (highly recommended for performance)[1]
    *   `ninja` (for compilation)[1]

If you are planning to run this in 2024–2025, ensure your environment is updated to the latest compatible `transformers` version, as noted in the repository's upgrade instructions[1]. For consumer hardware (e.g., RTX 3060/4060 12GB or higher), you should be able to run inference comfortably using 4-bit or 8-bit quantization[5].

**ChangeChat** is a vision-language model (VLM) specifically designed for interactive, bi-temporal remote sensing (RS) change analysis[1][2]. It enables tasks such as change captioning, classification, quantification, and localization by leveraging multimodal instruction tuning[3][2].

### Key Information
*   **GitHub Repository:** [hanlinwu/ChangeChat](https://github.com/hanlinwu/ChangeChat)[1][4]
*   **VRAM Requirements:** The repository explicitly recommends an NVIDIA GPU with **≥48GB VRAM** (with an **L20** GPU recommended) for running the model[5].

Research papers associated with ChangeChat (e.g., arXiv:2409.08582) typically fall under the [arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license](https://arxiv.org/licenses/nonexclusive-distrib/1.0/license.html)[6][7][8]. If you intend to use the code for commercial or redistribution purposes, you should check the repository's `LICENSE` file or contact the authors directly, as academic code repositories sometimes lack standard permissive licenses.

### Technical Context
*   **Architecture:** ChangeChat uses a pre-trained CLIP-ViT as its vision tower, a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) cross-modal adaptor, and the Vicuna-v1.5 model as the language model base[1][9]. 
*   **Training:** The model is fine-tuned using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA)[1][9]. It is associated with the **ChangeChat-87k** (and in some contexts, a 105k) instruction-following dataset[1][2][10].
*   **Related Work:** ChangeChat is often discussed alongside other remote sensing VLMs such as **DeltaVLM** (which uses the ChangeChat-105k dataset) and **BTCChat**[3][11][10].

The **CROMA** (Remote Sensing Representations with Contrastive Radar-Optical Masked Autoencoders) model, presented at NeurIPS 2023, is a framework designed for learning unimodal and multimodal representations from spatially aligned multispectral optical and synthetic aperture radar (SAR) data[1][2][3].

### Key Information & Requirements

*   **Official Repository:** The model code and documentation can be found in the official GitHub repository: [antofuller/CROMA](https://vertexaisearch.cloud.google.com/grounding-api-redirect/AUZIYQEtibE-kZpL5Dn-x9rAb9LWIxH6wk7CkDTZyE7hzUiIxxt9N89PmzAaYU03NrpZw14N6Rtq3M_zJr94pThhaI_P5OUqp7MN3SLLy0AWkgGVfCv2cb44gQUa7w==)[4].
*   **Data Requirements:** 
    *   The model is specifically designed for spatially and temporally aligned **multispectral optical imagery** (e.g., Sentinel-2) and **synthetic aperture radar (SAR) data** (e.g., Sentinel-1)[1][5].
    *   Sentinel-1 data typically involves VV and VH backscatter, while Sentinel-2 input usually includes 12 surface reflectance bands (with the cirrus band removed)[5].
*   **Hardware/Compute:** The original pretraining for CROMA-B and CROMA-L was conducted on high-performance compute clusters (e.g., NVIDIA DGX servers with 8× A100–80 GB GPUs)[5]. However, the model is structured to allow users to finetune encoders based on their specific task and data availability[5].
*   **Implementation:**
    *   The repository provides files like `use_croma.py` for loading pretrained models and `pretrain_croma.py` for training from scratch[6].
    *   The framework uses PyTorch[4][7].
    *   Users can leverage Hugging Face integration for easier loading of pretrained checkpoints[7][8].

### Summary of the Model
CROMA combines contrastive learning and reconstruction objectives[1][2]. It features separate Vision Transformer (ViT) encoders for radar and optical data, and a multimodal encoder that fuses these sensors for joint representation[9]. It also introduces **X- and 2D-ALiBi** (Attention with Linear Biases) to improve cross- and self-attention, enabling the model to handle images of varying sizes at test-time[1][10].

BigEarthNet is a widely used benchmark archive for remote sensing image analysis, featuring multi-modal data from Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 satellites. As of 2024, the dataset has been updated to **version 2.0**[1][2].

### Dataset Versions and Overview
*   **BigEarthNet v2.0:** This is the latest version, consisting of **549,488 pairs** of co-registered Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 image patches[1][3]. It improves upon v1.0 by using updated atmospheric correction (sen2cor v2.11) and more recent CORINE Land Cover (CLC2018 v2020_u1) labels[1][4].
*   **BigEarthNet v1.0:** The original archive contained **590,326 pairs** of image patches[5][6].

### Data Composition & Bands
The dataset provides multi-modal, multi-label data:
*   **Sentinel-2 (Optical):** Includes **12 spectral bands**[7].
    *   *Bands:* B01 (Coastal aerosol), B02 (Blue), B03 (Green), B04 (Red), B05, B06, B07 (Vegetation red edge), B08 (NIR), B8A (Narrow NIR), B09 (Water vapor), B11, B12 (SWIR)[8][7].
    *   *Resolutions:* Varies by band (10m, 20m, 60m)[8][9].
*   **Sentinel-1 (Radar):** Includes **2 bands** (VV and VH polarization)[7].

### Download Size
The storage requirements depend on the specific version and format being downloaded:
*   **BigEarthNet-S2 v1.0:** Approximately **66 GiB**[2].
*   **BigEarthNet-S1 v1.0:** Approximately **56 GiB**[2].
*   *Note:* TensorFlow Datasets (for v1.0) reports a total download size of roughly **65.22 GiB**[8][10]. The v2.0 dataset utilizes Zstandard compression to minimize storage space and speed up transfer[11].

### Training and Usage
*   **Labels:** The dataset is used primarily for multi-label classification[12]. While the original dataset contains 43 land-cover classes, many researchers map these to 19 broader categories[7][12].
*   **Accessibility:** You can access the data through the official [BigEarthNet website](https://bigearth.net/) or via platforms like Hugging Face (e.g., `GFM-Bench/BigEarthNet`) and TensorFlow Datasets[8][7][13].
*   **Recent Developments:** A newer variant, **BigEarthNet.txt**, was introduced in 2026, providing 464,044 co-registered image patches paired with 9.6 million text annotations to support vision-language models (VLMs)[14][15].

The field of **Change Detection Visual Question Answering (CDVQA)** in remote sensing has evolved significantly since its inception, moving from basic textual answering tasks to more complex frameworks that include visual grounding.

### Key Datasets and Benchmarks

*   **CDVQA (The Initial Dataset):** Introduced by Yuan et al. (2022)[1][2], this dataset was the pioneer in the field. It was constructed using an automatic question-answer generation method based on bi-temporal remote sensing images (often leveraging datasets like SECOND)[3][4][5]. It focuses on enabling non-expert users to query high-level semantic changes in Earth's surface via natural language[6].
*   **QAG-360K (CDQAG Benchmark):** A major development in 2024 is the introduction of **Change Detection Question Answering and Grounding (CDQAG)**[7][8]. This task extends traditional CDVQA by providing not only textual answers ("what has changed") but also intuitive visual evidence ("where has changed") through segmentation masks[8][9]. The **QAG-360K** dataset is the primary benchmark for this, containing over 360,000 triplets of questions, textual answers, and visual masks across 10 land-cover categories[7][10].
*   **BrightVQA:** A more recent dataset (noted in research from 2025/2026 contexts) designed to address domain generalization in CDVQA, focusing on performance stability when training and testing data distributions differ[11].

### Current Research Trends (2024–2025)
*   **VisTA Baseline:** Along with the QAG-360K dataset, researchers introduced the **VisTA** baseline model, which unifies question answering and visual grounding to achieve state-of-the-art results on both the classic CDVQA and the new CDQAG benchmarks[7][10].
*   **Vision-Language Models (VLMs):** Recent research has shifted toward evaluating modern multimodal models (e.g., Qwen-VL variants) on CDVQA tasks[12]. Studies indicate that native multimodal models often outperform traditional structured vision-language pipelines for semantic change reasoning[12].
*   **Advanced Architectures:** New approaches, such as the **Text-Conditioned State Space Model (TCSSM)**, are being explored to better handle domain shifts and integrate multi-temporal visual and textual features[13][11].

If you are looking for these datasets for research, the **QAG-360K** benchmark is a central resource for recent work in the field[7][2]. Many of these datasets are hosted on platforms like GitHub (e.g., under repositories for "Awesome-RS-VL-Data" or specific paper repositories)[2][14].

Consequently, it is distributed under the **Llama 2 Community License**, which permits commercial use, provided you comply with the specific terms and usage policies set by Meta.

While the base models are generally considered commercially permissive (under the Llama 2 Community License), there are several factors to keep in mind:

1.  **Training Data Restrictions:** Even if the model weights are under a permissive license, some components of the training pipeline—such as datasets generated by OpenAI (e.g., via GPT-4)—may have their own "Terms of Use" that restrict commercial competition or usage. This is why many organizations prefer to train their own versions or use commercially permissive datasets for fine-tuning.
2.  **Llama 2 Community License:** Ensure that your intended use complies with the specific requirements of the Llama 2 Community License (e.g., user base size limitations, attribution, and prohibited use cases).

The Smart India Hackathon (SIH) evaluation process is a rigorous, multi-stage journey designed to filter innovative, scalable, and technically sound solutions. Whether you are working on Remote Sensing or any other theme, the core evaluation framework remains consistent.

### **1. Evaluation Process Overview**
*   **Internal Hackathon:** Every participating college conducts an internal hackathon to select the best teams. Evaluators (often internal faculty or industry experts) use standardized criteria to nominate teams for the national level.
*   **Idea Submission & Shortlisting:** Nominated teams submit their idea proposals on the official SIH portal. These are reviewed by expert panels. Only the top-scoring teams per problem statement (typically 4–5) are selected for the **Grand Finale**.
*   **Grand Finale:** This is an offline event held at designated nodal centers. Teams present their working prototypes/models to a panel of judges.

### **2. Judging Criteria**
Judges generally score teams based on a weighted rubric (typically totaling 50–100 marks). Key parameters include:
*   **Novelty & Innovation (20–25%):** How unique is the solution compared to existing ones? Does it use technology in an creative way?
*   **Technical Implementation (20–25%):** Does the prototype work? Is the architecture sound? Did you handle errors and edge cases?
*   **Impact & Usefulness (20–25%):** Does it solve a real-world problem effectively? Is the target user clear, and is the impact measurable?
*   **Feasibility & Sustainability (15–20%):** Can this be deployed in the real world? Is it cost-effective and scalable?
*   **Presentation & Demo (15–20%):** Quality of your pitch, clarity of your slides, and the success of your live demonstration.

### **3. Demo & Presentation Format**
*   **Pitch Deck (PPT):** You must strictly follow the official SIH PPT template. Avoid extra slides, as this can lead to disqualification. Focus on the problem, your unique solution, system architecture, and a roadmap for future development.
*   **Live Demo:** A functional prototype is highly encouraged and carries significant weightage. A "live" demo (or a high-quality video if the demo is environment-dependent) that proves your core feature works is far superior to mockups.
*   **Q&A:** Expect a dedicated Q&A session where judges will challenge your technical choices, scalability, and security measures.

### **4. Remote Sensing & Specialized Themes**
For domains like **Remote Sensing, ISRO/Department of Space projects, or AI/ML-based imaging**, judges pay specific attention to:
*   **Data Integrity & Processing:** How you handle multispectral/hyperspectral data, edge processing, or sensor calibration.
*   **Practical Applicability:** Whether your remote sensing model can function under real-world constraints (e.g., low bandwidth, cloud cover, or specific geographic requirements).
*   **Technical Depth:** Ensure your solution clearly explains the algorithms used (e.g., CNNs for image classification, change detection, or feature extraction) and why they are appropriate for the specific problem statement.

### **Tips for Success**
*   **Solve the Right Problem:** Read the problem statement description thoroughly. Do not build a generic app when a specific analytical tool is requested.
*   **Architecture Matters:** For software solutions, provide clean, defensible architecture diagrams. For hardware, focus on the "how" of the mechanical/electronic design.
*   **Avoid Common Pitfalls:** Do not use placeholder content, ensure your team meets gender-balance requirements, and never copy solutions from previous winners (judges perform checks for this).

*   **Default Copyright:** Under GitHub's Terms of Service, while other users may have the right to view and fork public repositories, the lack of an open-source license means you do not have the legal right to use, modify, or redistribute the code or weights for your own purposes unless otherwise authorized by the author.
*   **Context on Datasets:** It is worth noting that related projects by the same or similar research groups (such as **DeltaVLM**, which is also associated with the same authors and datasets) sometimes specify licenses for their components (e.g., CC-BY-4.0 for annotations). However, this does not automatically extend to the ChangeChat repository or its weights.

If you intend to use the ChangeChat model weights or code for any project, you should contact the authors directly to request clarification on the terms of use or to ask them to publish a license.

The search for "rasterio GDAL co-registration satellite images Python alignment geotiff reprojection challenges" returned the following summary:
Co-registration of satellite imagery is a critical geospatial process that involves aligning two or more images of the same area taken at different times or by different sensors. In Python, **Rasterio** and **GDAL** are the foundational libraries for this task, though they serve different roles.

### Key Tools & Libraries
*   **Rasterio:** Provides a "Pythonic" interface to GDAL. It is excellent for reading, writing, and manipulating raster data, handling projections, and performing coordinate transformations.
*   **GDAL:** The underlying engine for most geospatial operations. While you can use GDAL's Python bindings directly, Rasterio is generally preferred for its cleaner API and better management of modern Python environments.
*   **Specialized Libraries:** For automated co-registration (which is often complex to build from scratch), libraries like **[AROSICS](https://github.com/GFZ/arosics)** are highly recommended as they are specifically designed to handle sub-pixel alignment of satellite imagery. For reprojecting and aligning stacks of images, **`rioxarray`** (which extends `xarray` with Rasterio/GDAL capabilities) is often used for its `reproject_match` method.

### Common Co-registration Workflow
Co-registration typically follows these steps:
1.  **Tie Point Identification:** Identify common, stationary features (e.g., road intersections, building corners) in both the reference and target images.
2.  **Transformation Calculation:** Use these tie points to calculate an Affine or polynomial transformation that maps the target image coordinates to the reference image coordinates.
3.  **Warping/Reprojection:** Apply the transformation to the target image (often using `gdalwarp` or `rasterio.warp`) to align it with the reference image.
4.  **Resampling:** Choose an appropriate resampling method (e.g., bilinear, cubic) to maintain data integrity during the warping process.

### Common Challenges
*   **Geometric Distortions:** Raw satellite images often contain distortions due to sensor angle (off-nadir viewing), Earth's curvature, and terrain relief. Without proper **orthorectification** (using a Digital Elevation Model), images may never align perfectly across different acquisitions.
*   **Coordinate System Mismatches:** Ensuring that both the reference and target rasters use the exact same Coordinate Reference System (CRS) and grid alignment is essential.
*   **Temporal/Environmental Changes:** Seasonal changes, cloud cover, or land-cover changes (e.g., new construction, vegetation growth) can make it difficult to find reliable, consistent tie points between two images.
*   **Data Consistency:** Different sensors or processing levels (e.g., Level 1 vs. Level 2 data) can have different pixel resolutions and radiometric properties, requiring careful resampling and pre-processing before alignment.
*   **Performance:** High-resolution satellite images can be massive (gigabytes in size). Using efficient methods like windowed reading or Cloud Optimized GeoTIFFs (COG) is necessary to avoid memory issues.

### Best Practices
*   **Avoid Mixing Libraries:** Do not import both `gdal` (the raw bindings) and `rasterio` in the same program if possible, as they can conflict due to how they manage underlying C-level objects and environment configurations.
*   **Use `reproject_match`:** When using `rioxarray`, the `reproject_match` function is a highly convenient way to force one raster to adopt the exact projection, resolution, and transform of another.
*   **Verify with Statistics:** Always evaluate your co-registration quality using Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) of your tie points or by performing visual change detection (e.g., calculating the absolute difference between images) to identify remaining misalignments.

# SatQuery AI — Build Specification v3: Comprehensive Risk & Issues Analysis

**Problem Statement ID:** 26167 | **Sponsor:** ISRO / SAC  
**Date:** 2026-09-20  

---

## Executive Verdict

The specification is **exceptionally well-engineered** — it is one of the most defensively architected hackathon plans I have seen. The deterministic-first philosophy, the license gate, the 3-hour budget cap on ChangeChat, the tiered BigEarthNet strategy, and the daily checkpoint discipline are all excellent risk-mitigation decisions.

**However**, several critical risks remain that could derail the project if not addressed proactively. This document catalogs every significant risk found, ordered by severity.

---

## ⚠️ CRITICAL RISKS (Could block demo or cause judge rejection)

---

### RISK 1 — GeoChat License Chain: The Hidden Vicuna/LLaMA Dependency

| Attribute | Detail |
|:--|:--|
| **Severity** | 🔴 CRITICAL |
| **Spec Section** | §4.1, §8.1, §13 |
| **Category** | Legal / Licensing |

**The Problem:**  
Your spec mandates a license gate for ChangeChat and CROMA, but treats GeoChat as the "primary specialist" without the same level of license scrutiny. Research reveals:

- **GeoChat** → Apache 2.0 (code & weights on HuggingFace)
- **BUT** GeoChat is fine-tuned from **LLaVA-1.5** → which uses **Vicuna-v1.5** → which is based on **Meta's Llama 2**
- Llama 2 Community License has **specific restrictions**: usage caps (>700M monthly active users need a separate license), acceptable use policy, and attribution requirements
- **Critically**: LLaVA's training data pipeline used **GPT-4 generated instruction data**. OpenAI's Terms of Service historically prohibited using their outputs to train competing models. This is a gray area that judges from ISRO/SAC could question.

**Mitigation:**  
- Apply the **same license gate** from §4.1 to GeoChat. Record the full chain: `GeoChat → LLaVA-1.5 → Vicuna-v1.5 → Llama 2 → Meta Community License` in `docs/model_licenses.md`
- Prepare a defense: SIH is a non-commercial academic competition, Llama 2 permits research use, and the GeoChat weights themselves are Apache 2.0
- Have a fallback plan if a judge challenges this (your capability registry already supports `demo_fallback`)

---

### RISK 2 — ChangeChat: Confirmed BLOCKED_LICENSE (No License File Exists)

| Attribute | Detail |
|:--|:--|
| **Severity** | 🔴 CRITICAL (but spec already mitigates this well) |
| **Spec Section** | §4.1, §8.2 |
| **Category** | Legal |

**The Problem:**  
Research confirms: **the `hanlinwu/ChangeChat` GitHub repository has NO LICENSE file**. Under default copyright law, you have **no legal right** to use, modify, or redistribute the code or weights. This is not a gray area — it is a clear legal blocker.

**Impact:**  
ChangeChat will almost certainly be `BLOCKED_LICENSE` when the license gate runs. This is exactly what your spec anticipated.

**Mitigation (already in spec, reinforce it):**  
- The deterministic change engine (§16) is correctly positioned as the primary path — this is your strongest architectural decision
- Template/rule-based explanations on top of verified masks/measurements are fully sufficient for the demo
- **Do NOT contact the authors asking for permission during the hackathon** — this wastes time and creates uncertainty. Accept the block and move on.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Your spec handles this perfectly. The only risk is if a team member ignores the license gate and integrates ChangeChat anyway. Enforce the gate procedurally.

---

### RISK 3 — GeoChat on Consumer GPU: The 14–16GB VRAM Reality

| Attribute | Detail |
|:--|:--|
| **Severity** | 🟠 HIGH |
| **Spec Section** | §3, §6, §8.1 |
| **Category** | Compute / Hardware |

**The Problem:**  
- GeoChat (7B params, LLaVA-1.5 base) needs **~14–16GB VRAM at FP16** for inference
- With **4-bit quantization**, it drops to **~6–8GB** but with quality degradation
- Your spec's Profile B (12–24GB consumer GPU) is marginal at full precision
- Many hackathon machines may be **Profile C (CPU only)**, making GeoChat completely unusable

**Impact:**  
If GeoChat is unavailable, you lose the primary implementation of:
- Single-image VQA (PS requirement #7)
- Grounding (PS requirement #8)
- The "remote-sensing-adapted VLM" requirement (#11)

The `demo_fallback` must be genuinely capable of answering remote-sensing VQA questions — not just returning "model unavailable."

**Mitigation:**
1. **Quantization strategy**: Implement 4-bit (BitsAndBytes/GPTQ) loading as default for Profile B. Test it on Day 3 before committing.
2. **Strengthen the demo_fallback**: The fallback for VQA must not be a stub. Options:
   - A lightweight RS-VQA model (e.g., a fine-tuned BLIP-2 or smaller VLM that fits in 4GB)
   - A rule-based system that uses NDVI/NDWI indices + land-cover classification to generate answers for common RS questions
   - Pre-computed responses for the demo dataset (honest but limited)
3. **Flash Attention**: The GeoChat repo recommends `flash-attn` — this is critical for reducing memory. Install it early.

---

### RISK 4 — BigEarthNet.txt Adaptation: The "Fine-Tuning" Requirement May Be Unachievable

| Attribute | Detail |
|:--|:--|
| **Severity** | 🟠 HIGH |
| **Spec Section** | §14, §15, PS requirement #12 |
| **Category** | ML / Training |

**The Problem:**  
- **BigEarthNet.txt** (2026) has **464,044 image pairs + 9.6M text annotations** — your Tier 1/2/3 strategy is correct to avoid downloading all of it
- However, the PS explicitly requires: *"At least one visual or vision-language component must be fine-tuned or otherwise adapted using BigEarthNet.txt or any open source training data"*
- LoRA/PEFT fine-tuning of GeoChat (7B params) requires:
  - **Minimum ~16GB VRAM** even with LoRA (rank 16, α=32)
  - **Hours of training time** even on a good GPU
  - Correct data loading pipeline matching GeoChat's expected input format (LLaVA conversation format)
- On Day 4 of an 8-day hackathon, you may not have stable GeoChat integration (Day 3) to fine-tune

**Impact:**  
If fine-tuning cannot complete, you cannot claim requirement #12 is satisfied. This is a **mandatory** PS requirement.

**Mitigation:**
1. **Broaden "adaptation" beyond LoRA fine-tuning**: The PS says "fine-tuned **or otherwise adapted**." This opens the door to:
   - **Prompt engineering with RS-specific few-shot examples** from BigEarthNet.txt metadata
   - **Feature adapter training**: Train only a small classification head on BigEarthNet features (much cheaper than full LoRA)
   - **Retrieval-augmented approach**: Index BigEarthNet.txt metadata and retrieve relevant examples at query time
2. **Use a smaller model for adaptation**: If GeoChat is too expensive to fine-tune, adapt a smaller model (e.g., a ResNet/ViT classifier) on BigEarthNet and register it as the "remote-sensing-adapted component"
3. **Record honestly**: As your spec says — if training cannot complete, report it. But have a concrete "adaptation" deliverable that isn't just "we tried and failed"

---

## 🟠 HIGH RISKS (Could significantly degrade demo quality)

---

### RISK 5 — Optical-SAR Fusion Engine: No Established Model, Must Be Built From Scratch

| Attribute | Detail |
|:--|:--|
| **Severity** | 🟠 HIGH |
| **Spec Section** | §8.4, §17 |
| **Category** | Architecture / ML |

**The Problem:**  
- Your spec correctly makes CROMA optional (trained on 8×A100-80GB — completely impractical for hackathon)
- But the **mandatory** Optical-SAR Fusion Engine must be built from scratch
- There is **no off-the-shelf library** that takes an arbitrary optical + SAR pair and produces fused analysis
- Building a credible fusion pipeline requires:
  - Correct handling of different spatial resolutions (Sentinel-2: 10/20/60m bands; Sentinel-1: typically 10m)
  - Radiometric normalization (optical reflectance vs. SAR backscatter in dB)
  - Meaningful index extraction (NDVI, NDWI, NDBI from optical; VV/VH ratio, texture from SAR)
  - Spatial overlay and comparison logic
  - Confidence estimation that is honest about what "fusion" actually means

**Impact:**  
A weak optical-SAR fusion demo will be immediately visible to ISRO/SAC judges who work with this data daily.

**Mitigation:**
1. **Start with Sentinel-1/Sentinel-2 pairs** (your spec already suggests this) — they are the most documented and standardized
2. **Define "fusion" conservatively**: Don't claim pixel-level fusion. Instead:
   - Optical → NDVI, NDWI, NDBI, land-cover evidence
   - SAR → backscatter classification (water = low VV+VH, urban = high VV, vegetation = moderate)
   - Fusion = spatial agreement/disagreement map between the two evidence layers
3. **Use AROSICS** for automated co-registration (much better than building from scratch)
4. **Budget Day 6 carefully** — this is a full day's work with no shortcuts

---

### RISK 6 — The 8-Day Schedule Is Extremely Aggressive

| Attribute | Detail |
|:--|:--|
| **Severity** | 🟠 HIGH |
| **Spec Section** | §27 |
| **Category** | Schedule |

**The Problem:**  
Each day's scope is ambitious:

| Day | Scope | Realistic Hours Needed | Hidden Complexity |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| 1 | Full FastAPI + React shell + upload + GeoTIFF parser + metadata + readiness gate + sample data acquisition | 12–16h | React/Next.js setup alone can consume 3–4h with dependency issues |
| 2 | Query contract + task schema + capability registry + router + execution trace + runtime mode | 8–12h | Designing the router to be genuinely agentic (not just if/else) is complex |
| 3 | GeoChat license gate + preflight + VQA + grounding integration | 10–14h | GeoChat's codebase has LLaVA-specific quirks; processor loading often fails silently |
| 4 | BigEarthNet manifest + subset + train/val split + LoRA pipeline + evaluation | 12–16h | Data pipeline + training loop + evaluation = a full research sprint |
| 5 | Deterministic change engine + registration + mask + measurement + (optional ChangeChat) | 10–14h | Co-registration of temporal pairs is non-trivial |
| 6 | Optical-SAR fusion from scratch | 10–14h | See Risk 5 |
| 7 | Evidence store + verification + numerical guard + reports + GUI polish | 12–16h | PDF generation + GeoJSON export + overlay rendering |
| 8 | Full acceptance suite + bug fixes + freeze | 8–12h | "Fix only bugs" always takes longer than expected |

**Total realistic estimate: 82–114 hours** for a single developer. For a team, coordination overhead adds ~20%.

**Mitigation:**
1. **Parallelize**: Assign frontend (Days 1, 7, 8), backend/router (Days 1, 2), ML (Days 3, 4), GIS (Days 5, 6) to different team members
2. **Have Day 1 infrastructure pre-built**: The FastAPI + React scaffold, GeoTIFF parser, and upload logic should be ready before the hackathon starts (pre-work is allowed for SIH)
3. **Cut scope honestly**: If Day 4 (fine-tuning) blocks, skip to Day 5 immediately. The deterministic change engine is more valuable to the demo than a partially-trained LoRA adapter.

---

### RISK 7 — React + FastAPI + PyTorch + GDAL: Dependency Hell

| Attribute | Detail |
|:--|:--|
| **Severity** | 🟠 HIGH |
| **Spec Section** | §5, §22 |
| **Category** | Environment / DevOps |

**The Problem:**  
The spec mandates:
- **Frontend**: React/Next.js (Node.js ecosystem)
- **Backend**: FastAPI (Python)
- **ML**: PyTorch + Transformers + PEFT + flash-attn
- **GIS**: Rasterio + GDAL + GeoPandas + Shapely + pyproj
- **Visualization**: Leaflet/OpenLayers/MapLibre
- **4 separate conda envs**: env-core, env-geochat, env-changechat, env-croma

**Specific known conflicts:**
- `GDAL` Python bindings are notoriously fragile — version must exactly match system GDAL
- `rasterio` and raw `gdal` Python bindings **should not coexist in the same environment** (the spec's research confirms this)
- `flash-attn` requires **CUDA toolkit headers** and fails on Windows frequently
- `env-geochat` will need specific `transformers` version pinning (GeoChat was built on an older version)
- Running 4 separate environments with inter-process communication adds latency and debugging complexity

**On Windows (your OS):**
- GDAL installation is significantly harder than on Linux
- `flash-attn` has **no official Windows support** (requires compilation from source or WSL)
- GeoChat's repo assumes Linux paths and shell scripts

**Mitigation:**
1. **Use WSL2** (Windows Subsystem for Linux) for all ML and GIS work — this is almost mandatory
2. **Use `conda-forge`** for GDAL/Rasterio — it handles binary dependencies correctly
3. **Simplify to 2 environments** in practice: `env-core` (FastAPI + Rasterio + GDAL) and `env-ml` (PyTorch + Transformers + GeoChat). The 4-env split is ideal but impractical under time pressure.
4. **Pin every dependency version** in `requirements/` files from Day 1
5. **Consider Docker** for the GeoChat service specifically — pre-built containers exist

---

### RISK 8 — Deterministic Change Engine: Co-Registration Is Harder Than It Looks

| Attribute | Detail |
|:--|:--|
| **Severity** | 🟠 HIGH |
| **Spec Section** | §8.3, §16 |
| **Category** | GIS / Algorithm |

**The Problem:**  
Your deterministic change pipeline assumes:
```
T1 + T2 → metadata validation → spatial registration → common grid → change computation
```

But real bi-temporal satellite imagery has:
- **Different CRS** (UTM zones vary by geography)
- **Sub-pixel misalignment** even with the same CRS
- **Different spatial resolutions** (Cartosat-2S: ~0.65m, Sentinel-2: 10m)
- **Radiometric differences** (different atmospheric conditions, sun angle, sensor calibration)
- **Seasonal vegetation changes** that are not "change events" but will trigger false positives

Simple pixel-differencing on misaligned images produces **noise, not change masks**.

**Mitigation:**
1. **Use AROSICS** (`pip install arosics`) for automated sub-pixel co-registration — it handles tie-point detection and transformation automatically
2. **Implement radiometric normalization** (histogram matching or relative radiometric normalization) before differencing
3. **Use morphological filtering** (opening/closing) on the raw difference to suppress noise
4. **Test on your Day-1 sample imagery** — don't wait until Day 5 to discover alignment issues
5. **For the demo**: Use pre-aligned Sentinel-2 time series from the same tile (e.g., same UTM zone, same processing level) to minimize co-registration issues

---

## 🟡 MODERATE RISKS

---

### RISK 9 — ISRO/SAC Hidden Evaluation Data: Cartosat-2S + RISAT Format Unknowns

| Attribute | Detail |
|:--|:--|
| **Severity** | 🟡 MODERATE |
| **Spec Section** | §24, PS Evaluation Criteria |
| **Category** | Evaluation |

**The Problem:**  
The PS states: *"The ISRO/SAC evaluation set will contain pre-georeferenced and co-registered Cartosat-2S optical and RISAT SAR image pairs."* But:
- You have **zero access** to this data during development
- Cartosat-2S is a **very high resolution (VHR)** sensor (~0.65m) — very different from Sentinel-2 (10m) that you'll develop against
- RISAT SAR may use C-band with different processing levels than Sentinel-1
- The GeoTIFF metadata structure from ISRO's internal processing pipeline may differ from Copernicus/ESA conventions

**Impact:**  
A system that works perfectly on Sentinel data may fail on ISRO's proprietary format during evaluation.

**Mitigation:**
1. **Make the GeoTIFF parser truly generic** — extract metadata from the file itself, never assume band names, resolution, or CRS
2. **Test with multiple GeoTIFF sources**: Sentinel-2, Landsat, any available VHR imagery
3. **Handle gracefully**: If a band name or metadata field is missing, log it and continue with available information — don't crash
4. **Build resolution-aware processing**: Your NDVI/NDWI extraction must work at any resolution, not just 10m

---

### RISK 10 — Query Contract: NLP Intent Classification Without a Language Model

| Attribute | Detail |
|:--|:--|
| **Severity** | 🟡 MODERATE |
| **Spec Section** | §11, §12 |
| **Category** | Architecture |

**The Problem:**  
The Query Contract must classify natural language into structured intent:
```json
{"intent": "temporal_change", "requires_temporal_pair": true, ...}
```

But if GeoChat is your only language model and it may be unavailable, how do you classify the query? Options:
- **Keyword matching**: Fragile, fails on paraphrased queries
- **Small classifier model**: Needs training data
- **External API** (OpenAI, etc.): Network dependency, cost, and judges may question why an "agentic RS system" outsources intent classification

**Mitigation:**
1. **Hybrid approach**: Use keyword/regex patterns for the 5–6 known task types (the PS gives representative queries — use them as templates), with a small sentence-transformer model as fallback
2. **`sentence-transformers`** (e.g., `all-MiniLM-L6-v2`, ~80MB) can embed queries and compare to task prototypes via cosine similarity — runs on CPU, no GPU needed
3. **Pre-encode the representative queries** from the PS as prototype embeddings for each task type

---

### RISK 11 — Report Generation: PDF + GeoJSON + Mask Export Complexity

| Attribute | Detail |
|:--|:--|
| **Severity** | 🟡 MODERATE |
| **Spec Section** | §23 |
| **Category** | Engineering |

**The Problem:**  
The spec requires generating: `report.pdf`, `result.json`, `execution_trace.json`, `evidence.geojson`, `change_mask.tif`. PDF generation in Python is notoriously finicky:
- `reportlab` is powerful but verbose
- `WeasyPrint` requires system-level dependencies (Cairo, Pango) that are hard to install on Windows
- Including map visualizations and overlay images in PDF requires careful layout

**Mitigation:**
1. **Use `fpdf2`** — pure Python, no system dependencies, supports images and tables
2. **Generate HTML first, then PDF** using `pdfkit` + `wkhtmltopdf` if more formatting is needed
3. **Prioritize JSON/GeoJSON exports** — these are machine-readable and technically more impressive to judges
4. **Budget this for Day 7**, not Day 8

---

### RISK 12 — Verification Engine: "Checking Numerical Consistency" Is Underspecified

| Attribute | Detail |
|:--|:--|
| **Severity** | 🟡 MODERATE |
| **Spec Section** | §19, §20 |
| **Category** | Architecture |

**The Problem:**  
The Numerical Guard and Verification Engine are excellent concepts, but the spec doesn't define:
- What "numerical consistency" means operationally (e.g., does area in km² match pixel count × resolution²?)
- How to detect when a model output contradicts computed evidence
- What thresholds trigger "uncertain" vs. "verified"

**Mitigation:**
1. **Define concrete verification rules**:
   - `area_km2 == pixel_count × (resolution_m)² / 1e6` (within 1% tolerance)
   - `bbox` coordinates must fall within input image bounds
   - `confidence` must be in [0.0, 1.0]
   - Temporal dates must satisfy `T1 < T2`
   - Model-generated text must not contain numbers not present in the evidence store
2. **Implement as a rule engine**, not a neural verifier — deterministic rules are more trustworthy and easier to debug

---

## 🟢 LOW RISKS (Manageable with awareness)

---

### RISK 13 — SIH Demo Format: Live Demo Under Pressure

| Attribute | Detail |
|:--|:--|
| **Severity** | 🟢 LOW |
| **Spec Section** | §28 |
| **Category** | Presentation |

Research shows SIH Grand Finale judges score on: Novelty (20–25%), Technical Implementation (20–25%), Impact (20–25%), Feasibility (15–20%), Presentation & Demo (15–20%).

**The Problem:**  
- Live demos fail. Networks drop. Models crash on unfamiliar inputs.
- ISRO judges will ask **pointed technical questions** about SAR calibration, VLM hallucination, and radiometric accuracy.

**Mitigation:**
1. **Pre-load all demo inputs** — never download during the demo
2. **Record a backup video** of every demo scenario working
3. **Have pre-computed outputs cached** — if the model fails live, show the cached result and explain what happened honestly
4. **Prepare for these specific judge questions:**
   - *"How do you calibrate SAR backscatter?"* → Answer: metadata-aware, not universal formula
   - *"What happens if the VLM hallucinates an area measurement?"* → Answer: Numerical Guard prevents it
   - *"Why not use EarthGPT?"* → Answer: Monolithic VLM, no verification layer, confirmed hallucination risk

---

### RISK 14 — Unicode Identifier Bug (§40): Already Addressed But Needs Enforcement

| Attribute | Detail |
|:--|:--|
| **Severity** | 🟢 LOW |
| **Spec Section** | §40 |
| **Category** | Code Quality |

The spec mentions Cyrillic "О" appearing where Latin "O" is intended. This suggests the team has already encountered this bug. 

**Mitigation:** Add a pre-commit hook or CI check that rejects non-ASCII characters in Python identifiers, JSON keys, and YAML keys.

---

## 📋 SPECIFICATION GAPS (Missing items that should be addressed)

---

### GAP 1 — No Explicit Error Recovery for Mid-Pipeline Failures

The spec handles input validation and model unavailability, but doesn't address:
- What happens if GeoChat loads successfully but **crashes during inference** on a specific image?
- What happens if the change engine produces a mask but the **measurement step fails** (e.g., missing CRS for area calculation)?

**Recommendation:** Add a `try/except` → `fallback` → `log` pattern at every pipeline stage, not just at the model-availability level.

---

### GAP 2 — No Latency Budget

The spec mentions logging latency but doesn't define acceptable limits. For a demo:
- Upload + metadata: < 3 seconds
- Query classification: < 1 second
- VQA inference: < 30 seconds (Profile B) / < 60 seconds (CPU fallback)
- Change detection: < 45 seconds
- Report generation: < 10 seconds

**Recommendation:** Define and display estimated time in the UI. Judges get impatient.

---

### GAP 3 — No Explicit Windows Compatibility Statement

The spec assumes Linux-style paths and tools. Your machine runs **Windows**. Key gaps:
- `flash-attn` has no native Windows support
- GDAL installation differs significantly
- Shell scripts (`scripts/*.py`) may use Linux-specific commands
- File paths use `\` not `/`

**Recommendation:** Add a "Platform" section to the spec: "Development on Windows via WSL2; deployment target: Linux."

---

### GAP 4 — No Team Role Assignment

The spec defines what to build but not **who builds what**. For an 8-day sprint, parallel work is essential.

**Recommendation:**
- **Developer A**: Frontend (React/Next.js) + API routes + report generation
- **Developer B**: Backend (FastAPI) + router + contracts + evidence store
- **Developer C**: ML (GeoChat + BigEarthNet adaptation + model management)
- **Developer D**: GIS (GeoTIFF parsing + co-registration + change engine + Optical-SAR fusion)

---

### GAP 5 — The Spec References "BigEarthNet.txt" But This Is a 2026 Dataset

Your dossier cites *"BigEarthNet.txt (arXiv:2603.29630, 2026)"* with 9.6M text annotations. This is very new. Risks:
- The dataset or its download links may be unstable
- The text annotation format may not be well-documented yet
- No established baselines exist for comparison

**Recommendation:** Have **BigEarthNet v2.0** (the established 2024 version, image-only, 549K pairs) as a backup. The PS says "BigEarthNet.txt **or** any open source training data" — you have flexibility here.

---

## 🏗️ OVERALL ASSESSMENT

| Category | Score | Notes |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Architectural Soundness** | ★★★★★ | Deterministic-first, fallback chains, capability registry — excellent |
| **Risk Awareness** | ★★★★★ | License gates, compute profiling, honest reporting — best-in-class for hackathon |
| **Schedule Realism** | ★★★☆☆ | Aggressive for 8 days; parallelization and pre-work are essential |
| **Compute Feasibility** | ★★★☆☆ | Depends entirely on available GPU; Profile C makes GeoChat impossible |
| **Licensing Defensibility** | ★★★★☆ | GeoChat chain needs documentation; ChangeChat correctly blocked |
| **GIS/RS Depth** | ★★★★☆ | Co-registration and SAR calibration need more concrete algorithms |
| **Evaluation Readiness** | ★★★☆☆ | Hidden ISRO data format is a wildcard; generic GeoTIFF handling is critical |

### Top 5 Actions Before Starting Day 1

1. **Run the license gate for ALL three models** and document the full chain in `docs/model_licenses.md`
2. **Set up WSL2** with conda-forge for GDAL/Rasterio — do this before anything else
3. **Acquire sample imagery now**: 1 Sentinel-2 optical, 1 Sentinel-1 SAR, 1 temporal pair, 1 co-registered pair
4. **Test GeoChat loading with 4-bit quantization** on your actual hardware — determine Profile before planning
5. **Pre-build the React + FastAPI scaffold** — don't waste Day 1 on boilerplate
